concepts.title: Where Quantum Speedups Come From (and the Types of Speedup)
concepts.simple_explanation: A framework for judging any application: a quantum algorithm may give an exponential-type speedup, a quadratic speedup, or no speedup, and the type decides whether it can matter in practice.
concepts.why_it_matters: "Quantum is faster" is meaningless without saying how much faster, for what, and on what hardware. A quadratic speedup on a slow, error-corrected machine may never beat a fast classical one; a super-polynomial speedup can change what is computable.
concepts.how_it_works:
Speedups are measured by how the number of steps grows with problem size N (or n bits). Types:
• Super-polynomial ("exponential-type"): e.g. Shor's factoring versus the best known classical factoring algorithms.
• Quadratic: e.g. Grover search, ~√N steps instead of ~N.
• Heuristic / no proven speedup: e.g. most optimization and machine-learning proposals; they may work well in practice, but nothing guarantees it.
Practical benefit also depends on overheads: error correction, clock speed, loading data in, and reading results out.
concepts.visual_explanation: A "speedup ladder": three rungs labelled super-polynomial, quadratic, heuristic, each with example problems, and a second axis showing "hardware needed" (small noisy → large fault-tolerant).
concepts.technical_explanation: Speedups are stated against the best known (or best possible) classical algorithm, and for some tasks (e.g. factoring) the classical comparison is "best known", not "proven optimal".
concepts.mathematical_representation:
Classical unstructured search ≈ N steps; Grover ≈ √N steps.
Factoring n-bit numbers: Shor ≈ polynomial in n; best known classical ≈ super-polynomial in n.
concepts.example: Doubling a problem's size doubles classical search time (~N) but multiplies Grover's time by only about √2.
concepts.common_mistake: Treating all quantum speedups as "exponential". Most proven ones in search are quadratic.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Extends Topic 1.2 C08 (what quantum computers are good at).
concepts.try_it: Place example problems on the speedup ladder (Activity A01).
concepts.key_takeaway: Ask three questions of any claimed application: how big is the speedup, against what classical method, and on what kind of hardware?

concepts.title: Cryptography: Shor's Algorithm and the Quantum Threat
concepts.simple_explanation: Shor's algorithm factors large integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time on an ideal quantum computer. Common public-key systems — RSA, Diffie–Hellman, and elliptic-curve cryptography — rely on these problems being hard for classical computers, so a large fault-tolerant quantum computer would break them.
concepts.why_it_matters: Public-key cryptography secures web connections, software updates, digital signatures and certificates. Data encrypted today could be recorded now and decrypted later once a capable quantum computer exists ("harvest now, decrypt later"), which makes migration planning urgent even before such a machine exists.
concepts.how_it_works:
Shor's algorithm reduces factoring to finding the period of a function; a quantum computer finds that period efficiently using superposition and interference (the Quantum Fourier Transform), which Topic 1.2 C05 previewed. Classical computers have no known efficient method.
Important limits:
• It requires a large, error-corrected quantum computer. A 2025 resource estimate by Gidney (Google Quantum AI) says factoring a 2048-bit RSA number could take fewer than one million noisy physical qubits and under a week, under stated assumptions (0.1% gate error, surface-code cycle of 1 µs, 10 µs reaction time). That is roughly 20× fewer qubits than the 2019 estimate of about 20 million qubits and 8 hours. It is an estimate, not a demonstration, and no machine of that size and quality exists today.
• Symmetric ciphers (e.g. AES) and hash functions are not broken by Shor. Grover's algorithm only provides a square-root speedup for brute-force key search.
concepts.visual_explanation: Two columns: "Broken by Shor (large fault-tolerant quantum computer)": RSA, Diffie–Hellman, ECC. "Weakened only quadratically by Grover": AES, SHA-family hashes (mitigate with longer keys/outputs).
concepts.technical_explanation: Shor's algorithm runs in time polynomial in the number of bits; the best known classical factoring algorithm (the general number field sieve) is sub-exponential but super-polynomial.
concepts.mathematical_representation:
Grover on a k-bit key: ~2^(k/2) steps instead of ~2^k.
AES-128: ~2¹²⁸ → ~2⁶⁴ (idealised); AES-256: ~2²⁵⁶ → ~2¹²⁸.
concepts.example: See E02: how Shor and Grover affect RSA, ECC, AES-128 and AES-256.
concepts.common_mistake: Saying "quantum computers will break all encryption". Only certain public-key schemes are broken; symmetric encryption just needs larger keys.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Applies Topic 1.2's interference idea and its note that Shor's algorithm gives a large speedup while Grover's is quadratic.
concepts.try_it: Use the key-strength calculator (Activity A03) to compare classical and quantum-attack strength.
concepts.key_takeaway: Shor's algorithm threatens public-key cryptography; Grover's algorithm only halves the effective bit-strength of symmetric keys. No machine capable of breaking RSA-2048 exists today.

concepts.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
concepts.simple_explanation: PQC means classical cryptographic algorithms designed to stay secure against both classical and quantum attackers. QKD is a different idea: using quantum physics to distribute encryption keys, which needs quantum hardware and communication links.
concepts.why_it_matters: PQC is the main practical response to the quantum threat, and it runs on today's ordinary computers. Learners often confuse it with QKD, or think defending against quantum computers requires a quantum computer.
concepts.how_it_works: PQC schemes rely on mathematical problems with no known efficient quantum attack (for example problems on lattices, hash functions or error-correcting codes). NIST published its first PQC standards in August 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, key establishment), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA, signatures) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA, hash-based signatures). A further signature standard (FIPS 206, based on FALCON) was still in development at the time of checking, and NIST selected HQC in March 2025 as an additional key-establishment algorithm. QKD (the first protocol is BB84, 1984) uses quantum states to establish keys whose eavesdropping can be detected, but it needs specialised hardware and still requires classical authentication.
concepts.visual_explanation: A comparison diagram: PQC = new maths, runs on normal computers, software upgrade; QKD = quantum hardware and links, physics-based key exchange.
concepts.technical_explanation: PQC security is based on computational hardness assumptions (not proven unconditionally); algorithms undergo years of public cryptanalysis, and some candidates have been broken classically in the past, which is why standardisation is slow and cautious.
concepts.example: A web server can adopt ML-KEM for key exchange through a software update; no quantum hardware is involved.
concepts.common_mistake: Thinking "post-quantum" means "uses quantum computers" or that PQC and QKD are the same thing.
concepts.try_it: Sort statements into "PQC", "QKD", or "both" (Activity A03, part 2).
concepts.key_takeaway: Post-quantum cryptography is classical software designed to resist quantum attacks; it is available as standards today. QKD is a separate, hardware-based approach.

concepts.title: Simulating Quantum Systems: Chemistry and Materials
concepts.simple_explanation: Using a quantum computer to model the behaviour of molecules, catalysts, and materials — for example to compute their energy levels — directly with quantum states.
concepts.why_it_matters: This is widely regarded as the most natural application: the idea goes back to Richard Feynman in the early 1980s, who argued that simulating quantum physics on classical computers is inefficient while a quantum computer could do it naturally. Better simulation could help with understanding catalysts, batteries, drug-target interactions and new materials.
concepts.how_it_works:
The state of a quantum system with n relevant quantum degrees of freedom needs ~2ⁿ amplitudes on a classical computer (Topic 1.2 C06). A quantum computer with roughly n qubits (in standard encodings, about one qubit per electronic orbital state) can hold such a state natively. Algorithms such as quantum phase estimation can compute ground-state energies with provable guarantees on fault-tolerant hardware; **hybrid variational algorithms** such as the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) use short noisy circuits plus a classical optimiser and are designed for current devices, but their advantage over classical methods is unproven.
Honest status: small molecules have been simulated on quantum hardware; useful, classically-intractable chemistry is expected to need fault-tolerant machines. Resource estimates for practically relevant molecules vary by orders of magnitude, and improved classical methods keep raising the bar quantum computers must clear.
concepts.visual_explanation: A molecule on the left with its electron orbitals; on the right, qubits representing orbitals; a growing "classical memory needed" bar versus a "qubits needed" bar.
concepts.technical_explanation: The goal is typically the ground-state energy of a Hamiltonian H. The variational principle guarantees that any trial state's energy is ≥ the true ground-state energy, which VQE exploits.
concepts.mathematical_representation: E(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)| H |ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀ ;  VQE minimises E(θ) over θ.
concepts.example: See E03 (state-space size) and E04 (a one-qubit variational toy example).
concepts.common_mistake: Saying "quantum computers can simulate anything faster". The natural advantage is for quantum systems; many classical systems (weather, traffic) have no known quantum speedup.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Directly applies the 2ⁿ state-space growth from Topic 1.2.
concepts.try_it: Slide the number of orbitals and compare classical memory with qubit count (Visual V04), then run the toy variational loop (Activity A04).
concepts.key_takeaway: Simulating quantum systems is the strongest, most natural application case, but useful large-scale results are expected to need fault-tolerant quantum computers.

concepts.title: Search, Sampling and Estimation (Grover and Relatives)
concepts.simple_explanation: Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among N unsorted items in about √N steps; related "amplitude amplification/estimation" methods give a similar quadratic speedup for some counting and Monte Carlo estimation tasks.
concepts.why_it_matters: Searching a huge space is common (cryptanalysis, constraint problems, estimation in finance and science). A quadratic speedup is real but modest, and overheads can erase it.
concepts.how_it_works:
Grover's algorithm repeatedly applies two steps that, through interference, raise the amplitude of the marked item while lowering the others (Topic 1.2 C05, M02). It is provably optimal: no quantum algorithm can do unstructured search faster than order √N.
Practical caveats: (a) the speedup is only quadratic; (b) error correction makes each quantum step much more expensive than a classical step; (c) the "oracle" that recognises the right answer must itself be implemented as a circuit; (d) if the search space has structure, a classical algorithm may beat brute force by far more than √N.
concepts.visual_explanation: A bar chart of amplitudes: initially all equal, then the marked item's bar grows over repeated iterations (animation), with an iteration counter next to a classical "checks so far" counter.
concepts.technical_explanation: For one marked item among N, about (π/4)√N Grover iterations are needed; stopping too early or too late reduces the success probability.
concepts.mathematical_representation: Iterations ≈ (π/4)·√N ;  classical expected checks ≈ N/2 (worst case N).
concepts.example: See E01: N = 1,000,000 → about 785 Grover iterations versus about 500,000 expected classical checks.
concepts.common_mistake: Thinking Grover's algorithm makes NP-complete problems easy. It reduces brute-force search time by a square root, which is still exponential for exponentially large search spaces.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Builds on interference (Topic 1.2 C05) and the "tries all possibilities" misconception (M02).
concepts.key_takeaway: Grover gives a proven but quadratic speedup for unstructured search; it is useful, but not a magic key to hard problems.

concepts.title: Optimization and Machine Learning: Promise vs Proof
concepts.simple_explanation: Optimization (logistics, scheduling, portfolio choice) and machine learning are frequently cited as quantum applications. Approaches include quantum annealing, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), and quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms.
concepts.why_it_matters: These areas get the most commercial attention, so learners need to separate demonstrated results from marketing. Being cautious here is a sign of understanding, not pessimism.
concepts.how_it_works:
• Optimization: heuristic quantum methods (QAOA, annealing) explore solutions using superposition and interference, but there is no general proof that they beat the best classical heuristics on practical problems. Because NP-hard optimization problems are not known to be efficiently solvable by quantum computers, any gain is expected to be limited (e.g. quadratic, or heuristic and instance-specific).
• Machine learning: some proposed QML algorithms promise large speedups, but these often depend on assumptions that are hard to satisfy: loading classical data into a quantum state can itself take as long as the computation; reading results out gives limited information; and several proposed speedups were later matched by new classical ("dequantised") algorithms, e.g. for recommendation systems.
• Estimation: amplitude-estimation methods give a quadratic speedup in some Monte Carlo estimation tasks, relevant in principle to finance, but needing large fault-tolerant machines.
concepts.visual_explanation: A "claim checklist" graphic: data in → quantum algorithm → result out, with warning icons on the data-loading and read-out steps; alongside a column "classical baseline improved?".
concepts.technical_explanation: The "fine print" principle: a quantum speedup claim must be checked for input cost, output cost, the classical baseline used, and the hardware assumed.
concepts.example: A paper claims a quantum algorithm solves a linear-algebra step exponentially faster; but if the input matrix must be loaded entry by entry, the loading time can dominate and remove the advantage.
concepts.common_mistake: Assuming quantum computers will train neural networks or solve logistics problems "exponentially faster".
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Applies the limits stated in Topic 1.2 (M02–M04) to concrete application claims.
concepts.try_it: Use the claim-checklist activity (A01, part 2) on a made-up headline.
concepts.key_takeaway: For optimization and machine learning, quantum advantage is an open research question; judge claims by the fine print.

concepts.title: Hybrid Quantum–Classical Computing
concepts.simple_explanation: Most practical quantum workflows pair a quantum processor with classical computers (CPUs/GPUs/supercomputers). The classical side prepares inputs, optimises parameters, processes results and applies error mitigation; the quantum side runs the parts it is suited for.
concepts.why_it_matters: Quantum computers will not replace classical computers (Topic 1.2). They are expected to act as accelerators for specific sub-tasks, much as GPUs are today.
concepts.how_it_works: Variational algorithms (VQE, QAOA) loop: the classical optimiser proposes parameters θ → the quantum computer prepares a state and measures many shots → the classical computer updates θ. Even fault-tolerant machines need heavy classical processing for error-correction decoding and for pre-/post-processing.
concepts.visual_explanation: A loop diagram with a "classical optimiser" box and a "quantum processor" box connected by arrows labelled "parameters θ" and "measurement results".
concepts.technical_explanation: Noisy-device workflows trade circuit depth for repeated runs and classical post-processing.
concepts.mathematical_representation: θ_(k+1) = Optimiser(θ_k, E(θ_k)), where E(θ) is estimated from measured shots.
concepts.example: E04's one-qubit example is a miniature variational loop.
concepts.common_mistake: Imagining a quantum computer as a standalone replacement for a data centre.
concepts.connection_to_previous_concepts: Reinforces Topic 1.2: quantum devices are specialised, noisy, and probabilistic (many shots needed).
concepts.try_it: Run the variational loop in A04 and watch the energy fall to its minimum.
concepts.key_takeaway: Practical quantum computing is hybrid: classical computers do most of the work and call on quantum processors for specific tasks.

concepts.title: Readiness: Noisy Devices, Fault Tolerance, and Reading "Quantum Advantage" Claims
concepts.simple_explanation: A way to judge how close each application is to reality: today's devices are noisy and limited; large, reliable (fault-tolerant) machines are needed for most high-value applications; "quantum advantage" claims must be read carefully.
concepts.why_it_matters: Applications are often described as if hardware were already ready. Learners should know the gap and the reasons progress is real yet uncertain.
concepts.how_it_works:
• Noisy intermediate-scale ("NISQ") devices: tens to hundreds or more of physical qubits with errors that limit circuit size. Useful for experiments, benchmarks and algorithm research.
• Fault-tolerant devices: many physical qubits combine into each error-corrected logical qubit. Experiments have shown that making the error-correcting code larger can reduce the logical error rate (the "below threshold" result, Google Quantum AI), and in 2026 IBM and collaborators reported a computation using 70 logical qubits. These are milestones, not yet the machines needed for Shor-scale factoring or large-scale chemistry.
• "Quantum advantage" means a quantum computer solves some task beyond the reach of the best classical methods. Claims are tested by new classical algorithms, and some have been narrowed or challenged after publication (the 2019 Google "supremacy" experiment was followed by improved classical simulations). Strong claims therefore need verification that the quantum result is correct and a comparison with the best classical baselines. Advantage on a contrived benchmark is not the same as useful advantage on a real-world problem.

raw_source: Readiness: Noisy Devices, Fault Tolerance, and Reading "Quantum Advantage" Claims

A way to judge how close each application is to reality: today's devices are noisy and limited; large, reliable (fault-tolerant) machines are needed for most high-value applications; "quantum advantage" claims must be read carefully.
Applications are often described as if hardware were already ready. Learners should know the gap and the reasons progress is real yet uncertain.
• Noisy intermediate-scale ("NISQ") devices: tens to hundreds or more of physical qubits with errors that limit circuit size. Useful for experiments, benchmarks and algorithm research.

• Fault-tolerant devices: many physical qubits combine into each error-corrected logical qubit. Experiments have shown that making the error-correcting code larger can reduce the logical error rate (the "below threshold" result, Google Quantum AI), and in 2026 IBM and collaborators reported a computation using 70 logical qubits. These are milestones, not yet the machines needed for Shor-scale factoring or large-scale chemistry.

• "Quantum advantage" means a quantum computer solves some task beyond the reach of the best classical methods. Claims are tested by new classical algorithms, and some have been narrowed or challenged after publication (the 2019 Google "supremacy" experiment was followed by improved classical simulations). Strong claims therefore need verification that the quantum result is correct and a comparison with the best classical baselines. Advantage on a contrived benchmark is not the same as useful advantage on a real-world problem.
